title: The Expanding Universe: Hubble and Redshift

cards.b: For most of history people assumed the universe was eternal and unchanging. In the 1920s the evidence showed otherwise: galaxies are flying apart. If they move apart now, they were closer before. Winding the film back leads to a beginning, the Big Bang.

Between 1912 and 1920s, Vesto Slipher measured spectra of spiral 'nebulae' and found most were redshifted: moving away fast. Their speeds were far greater than the stars in our galaxy. The nature of the nebulae was still debated.

In 1924 Edwin Hubble found Cepheid variables in Andromeda and showed it lay about a million light-years away (the modern value is about 2.5 million), well outside the Milky Way: these were separate galaxies. In 1929 he combined distances with redshifts and found that the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes.

The relation is v = H0 x d: recession speed v equals distance d times the Hubble constant H0, now about 70 km/s per megaparsec. A galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at about 7,000 km/s. Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian priest and physicist, predicted and estimated this in 1927 from Einstein's equations, two years before Hubble. In 2018 the IAU voted to call it the Hubble-Lemaitre law.

Galaxies are not flying through space from a centre. Space itself is stretching, like dots on an inflating balloon or raisins in rising dough: from any raisin, all others recede, and the farther ones faster. So there is no centre and no edge. Light waves are stretched along the way, producing cosmological redshift, which differs from the ordinary Doppler shift.

Redshift z measures the stretch: 1 + z is the factor by which the universe has expanded since the light left. A galaxy at z = 1 is seen when the universe was half its present size. Running the expansion backward, 1/H0 gives roughly 14 billion years, close to the real age, 13.8 billion years.

Measuring H0 is hard. Cepheids and supernovae in nearby galaxies (the SH0ES team, Adam Riess) give about 73 km/s/Mpc. The CMB analysed with the standard model (Planck) gives about 67 to 68. This Hubble tension is over 5 sigma, and may be a hint of new physics or hidden errors. It remains unresolved as of 2025.

• 'Galaxies fly away from a centre.' There is no centre.
  • 'Everything expands, including us.' Gravity or electromagnetic forces hold galaxies, atoms and you together; only the space between clusters grows.
  • 'Redshift always means motion through space.' At great distances it is stretching of space.

Jayant Narlikar worked with Fred Hoyle on the steady-state and the Hoyle-Narlikar gravity theories, rivals to the Big Bang. The CMB evidence settled the debate in favour of the Big Bang, but the rival ideas pushed the field to test hard. IUCAA and TIFR astronomers analyse supernova and galaxy-survey data to measure expansion. The uGMRT maps redshifted hydrogen emission from distant galaxies.

• Galaxies recede with speeds proportional to distance: v = H0 x d.
  • Space itself stretches; there is no centre of expansion.
  • Redshift measures how much the universe has grown since the light left.
  • The Hubble tension shows two methods disagree on H0.

Think about it: (1) Why does the law imply a beginning? (2) Why do galaxies not expand with space?
